feedback: If the child tries to 'take away' the larger from the smaller or reverses the rows to keep it 'takeable': re-align the two rows one-to-one and point only to the unmatched tail as the answer.
Reinforce by lining the rows up physically so the matched pairs and the leftover tail are visually clear.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction also answers comparison/difference questions ('how many more'), not only 'take away'. Meeting difference early is intended to help prevent the long-run difficulty of not recognising comparison problems as subtraction.
learnerActions: Line up two rows of objects, one under the other, matching them one-to-one.
Find the unmatched tail — the objects in the longer row with no partner.
Count that leftover tail to answer 'how many more does this row have?'
Connect it back: this 'how many more' is also a subtraction.
activities.title: Difference mode: 'how many more?' as subtraction

feedback: If the child is stuck, let them act it out with real objects: start from the whole, remove groups, and check which removal leaves the remaining amount.
Keep the missing-number idea grounded in action rather than as abstract symbol manipulation at this age.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction can ask for the unknown part that was taken away — an early concrete seed for missing-number forms (e.g. 5 − ? = 3, or 3 = 5 − ?) and for subtraction-and-addition as inverse actions. Acting it out also counters reading a written statement as a bare left-to-right instruction with no sense of the quantities involved.
learnerActions: See the starting group (e.g. 5) and the remaining group (e.g. 3), with the taken pile hidden or covered.
Work out how many must have been removed to leave what's there.
Act out or check by uncovering the hidden pile.
Say it as a missing-part sentence, e.g. '5 − ? = 3'.
activities.title: Mystery removed: reason back to the missing part
